subject: Is it possible to model the structured zero probability?

messages.author: ff1a5632abbf2fe9
messages.subject: Is it possible to model the structured zero probability?
parts:
Dear INLA experts


After reading the help of zero-inflated likelihood, I find in zero-inflated Poisson likelihood, instead of modeling zero probability with covariates, we can only treat the zero probability as a fixed unknown parameter.
Am I right? If yes, is there any trick to overcome this problem?


Thanks in advance
Best,
Xing

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Is it possible to model the structured zero probability?
parts:
On Sun, 2013-09-08 at 00:14 -0700, Zhao Xing wrote:
> Dear INLA experts
>
>
>
>
> After reading the help of zero-inflated likelihood, I find in
> zero-inflated Poisson likelihood, instead of modeling zero probability
> with covariates, we can only treat the zero probability as a fixed
> unknown parameter.
> Am I right? If yes, is there any trick to overcome this problem?

You're right. There is currently no way to overcome this problem, as it
makes the observation y_i depends on two linear predictors (one of the
poisson part and one of the zero-prob part).

It is possible to define special versions, if the model for the
zero-prob is simple and this would lead to a model that has general
interest. It needs to be simple as these parameters will be treated as
hyperparameters, hence conditionally on these, then all is fine.

Best
H


--
Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org

messages.author: 9a89594e7fcb7aad
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Is it possible to model the structured zero probability?
parts:
Elias reminded me of the following. The type0-models can be dealt with
using one linear predictor for the zero-probability and one for the mean
in the Poisson, say. It is a little complicated so we'll provide an
example

anyway, if the likelihood is

p 1[y=0] + (1-p) P(y; \eta | y > 0)

then create

z = 1 if y=0
= 0 if y=1

so this is a binary model for 'z' which is the model for the probability
'p'.

then add for all y such that y > 0, the type0 likelihood where 'p' is
fixed to be essentially zero. this will give a contribution P(y; \eta |
y > 0).



H
